First, the revolutionary method for understanding the heritage.
Second, the picture of the heritage revealed by that revolutionary method, as compared with the picture produced by other methods.
If we describe a method of understanding the heritage as revolutionary, it must rest on an intellectual foundation that expresses a revolutionary ideology.

We have already established that every understanding of the heritage begins from intellectual assumptions that form its ideological basis. For that reason, there can never be only one way of understanding the heritage. In a class society, there are as many forms of understanding as there are competing ideologies.
Each class has its ideology, and each ideology produces a particular way of understanding the heritage.

A revolutionary ideology is the ideology of the revolutionary forces within a society: the classes and social groups whose interests and ambitions, at a particular historical moment, are tied to the demand for revolutionary change.

By revolutionary change we mean the transformation of economic, social, and political conditions and institutions that can no longer meet the demands of development and progress in the interests of the most advanced social forces. These are the forces that play the central role in society’s material and intellectual production.

If we return to the basic content of the Arab liberation movement in its present stage, as we defined it earlier, we can say that the immediate requirements of revolutionary change are expressed in the achievement of a national-democratic revolution. Once its tasks are completed, this will provide the foundation and starting point for the socialist revolution.

At this particular moment in Arab history, the social and political forces objectively and subjectively capable of carrying out the national-democratic revolution are the progressive, national, and democratic forces joined in alliance: parties, organizations, institutions, and individuals united by broadly shared short-term goals, and in some cases by common long-term goals as well.

But the question that concerns us here is the place of scientific revolutionary thought within this alliance, and the place of the progressive forces that use this thought to guide their political activity and struggle.

Looking realistically at the Arab revolutionary movement at its present level of development, we can say that scientific revolutionary thought and the forces that put it into practice already occupy a particularly active place within the movement. They also benefit from favorable internal and external conditions—national, Arab, and international—which are helping them move with increasing momentum toward a position from which they can play a decisive role in determining the movement’s direction.
Seen in this light, the central ideology of the Arab revolutionary movement in its present historical stage becomes clearer.

It is the ideology of the movement’s basic forces: the classes and social groups that are most revolutionary and that have the greatest need for a transformation reaching down to the foundations of the existing economic, social, and political order.

These forces suffer from many forms of material and spiritual hardship. At the same time, they face national oppression, the seizure of their land and wealth, and the loss of control over their homeland and its history through imperialism and Zionism.
The scientific revolutionary thought of this ideology is, specifically, the thought of scientific socialism, with its two main foundations: dialectical materialism and historical materialism.
Of these two, historical materialism provides the basic method for producing a revolutionary understanding of the heritage.
B — The Picture of the Heritage
What picture of the heritage emerges from the method of historical materialism?

Its main outlines become clear through a dialectical view of the relationship between present and past, and of the relationship between our modern understanding of the heritage and the intellectual and social content of the heritage itself.
For our purposes, this dialectical view rests on two objective facts.
The first is that our understanding of the heritage is produced by contemporary science and contemporary ideology.

The second is that although this understanding begins from the standpoint of the present, both scientifically and ideologically, it can understand the heritage only by seeing it in its own historical setting.

In other words, we must understand the heritage as something that moved and developed within the historical time to which it belonged. More precisely, we must understand it through its relationship with the earlier social structure that produced it, and with the historical conditions that in turn produced that social structure, with all the particular features of that society and that age.
At first, these two facts may seem to contradict one another.

If we understand the heritage from the standpoint of the present, does that not mean dragging the past into the present? And would that not contradict our insistence that the heritage must be understood within its own historical setting?
This apparent contradiction comes from confusing two very different things: using modern knowledge to understand the heritage, and modernizing the heritage itself.
There is no necessary connection between them.

In practice, it is modern traditionalism that tries to make this connection. It pulls concepts from the past into the present by claiming that all the knowledge of our own age was already present in the past, that the past contained the same ideas we have today but expressed them in different language, and that nothing in modern knowledge is truly absent from the heritage.
This attempt to “modernize” the heritage has become increasingly common in recent years among some thinkers of the Arab bourgeoisie.

They are driven by an urgent need to repair a collapsing ideology and repaint it in bright “modern” colors while preserving its original substance: the class concepts that imply that the bourgeoisie can continue to exist forever as a class.

Quite apart from the class interests behind it and the illusion that bourgeois society can exist eternally, this attempt to modernize the heritage by treating past and present concepts as essentially identical directly contradicts the historical-materialist method of understanding the relationship between present and past.
The philosophical position behind this approach is, as we have already said, a metaphysical or static view of history. It imagines history moving in an empty circle.

Historical materialism, by contrast, sees history as moving in an upward spiral. That movement is governed by the general laws of human social development, interacting with the internal laws that shape the development of each particular society.
The idea of “modernizing” the heritage is therefore fundamentally different from our own proposal: to use contemporary scientific methods to produce new knowledge about the heritage.

The first major difference is that the bourgeois approach projects the past onto the present. It treats the present as nothing more than a continuation of the past—a rigid, metaphysical continuation that ultimately makes past and present identical.

We see their relationship as one of historical development, whose content includes both continuity and breaks, as quantitative changes give way to qualitative ones within the constant movement of history.
The second difference can be seen by comparing two very different goals.

The first approach tells us that we should “take from the ancients their points of view after separating them from the particular problems they were discussing,” and that we should “look at things in the same way they did. Or, to put it differently, we should judge our solutions to our problems by the same standards that they used.”

Our own approach, based on historical materialism, understands “the problem of our position toward the heritage” as “the problem of the relationship between thought within this present social structure and the thought that preceded it within an earlier social structure.”
Our aim, then, is not to “take from the ancients their points of view after separating them from their particular problems.”
The issue is not whether we should take ideas from the ancients or refuse to take them.
The real question is to determine “the form in which present thought understands its relationship with past thought”—that is, “the form in which this thought reveals itself to that thought.”
And we must do this without separating past thought from the particular problems the ancients themselves were trying to solve.
In fact, the opposite is required.
We need to see the thought of the ancients alive, with its flesh and blood still on it.

If we strip their thought of “their particular problems,” we strip it of its life, its flesh, and its blood. We remove its human dimensions. We destroy the vitality it had as a form of thought connected with a particular kind of social activity at a particular moment in history.
In the end, we also strip it of its value as heritage.
That is the first side of the question.
The second is that we need to approach the heritage in a way that allows us to achieve two goals.
First, we need to understand the heritage in a new way.

Second, we need to use this new understanding to help free contemporary Arab thought from its dependence on colonial thought and bourgeois ideology, which have historically become intertwined within the modern Arab social structure.
We have already explained many of the methodological and scientific principles involved in developing this new understanding.
As for how we put that understanding to use, the first requirement is to place the heritage back into its historical setting.
We must see it as the intellectual expression of medieval Arab-Islamic society, connected to the particular history of that society and to the complete structure of its material life.

If we place the heritage within that framework, using the scientific tools available to us today and approaching it from our revolutionary ideological position within present Arab society, we can begin to uncover the real social sources and origins of our intellectual heritage.

This allows us to develop a scientific view not only of the social forces that struggled against one another within that society, with all their specific historical features, but also of the intellectual and ideological forms taken by those struggles.
And we can understand those forms as historically specific forms, shaped by the level that human knowledge had reached at the time.
This allows us, first, to uncover the real relationship between the heritage and the historical conditions in which it arose.

Second, it allows us to uncover the objective relationship between the present Arab liberation movement and both the revolutionary and non-revolutionary elements within the movement of medieval Arab-Islamic history.
The main purpose of this double discovery is to reveal the historical dimensions of the present Arab revolutionary movement.
It allows us to see the elements of continuity between its earlier historical dimensions and its new dimensions in the present. It gives its modern character a sense of historical rootedness.
In other words, it allows us to see authenticity and modernity not as opposites, but as things that can exist together and interact.
This directly challenges the illusion, deeply reinforced by colonial thought and by Arab bourgeois thought, that authenticity and modernity must necessarily conflict.
When we use our understanding of the heritage in this way, we reach an especially important conclusion.
The heritage stops being a question about the past for its own sake. It also stops being an attempt to impose the past on the present.
Instead, it becomes a question about the present itself.

We reach this point by seeing the present as part of an ongoing process of change in which the achievements of the past and the possibilities of the future interact dynamically and move development forward.

There may be breaks in this process. Some arise from the dialectical character of historical development itself. Others are forced interruptions imposed by forces hostile to the content of the present Arab revolutionary movement.

Once we understand the heritage and the use of that understanding in this way, it becomes clear that the issue is not, as others have claimed, that we should “judge our solutions to our problems by the same standards that they”—the ancients—“used.”
That way of thinking is both unhistorical and irrational.
There are two connected reasons for this.
First, the problems faced by the ancients differ from the problems we face today because their historical conditions differed from ours.
Second, the “standards” they used grew out of those particular problems and conditions.
And as we have said, their problems and conditions were neither identical nor even similar to ours.
Their standards were also shaped by the relatively limited development, in their age, of the tools, material, and forms of knowledge available to them.
Those standards were therefore appropriate to that historical level of knowledge. They are not appropriate to the level knowledge has reached in our own time.
Our standards must therefore differ from theirs as well.
How, then, could it make sense for us to solve our problems by returning to the very same standards used by the ancients?
Our present has moved far beyond them. The distance involved cannot be measured simply in years.

What matters much more is the enormous difference between the nature of their problems and ours; between the economic, social, and political conditions of medieval Arab-Islamic civilization and those of our own age; and between the level and forms of consciousness available in their society and those available in Arab society today.

Once we see the difference between our method of approaching the heritage and the older and newer forms of traditionalism, we can also see the difference between the picture of the heritage produced by our method and the pictures produced by those traditionalist approaches, despite the differences among their theoretical currents.
The traditionalist picture of the heritage is generally marked by an emphasis on supernatural, idealist, and fatalistic thought.
Arab-Islamic society therefore appears in this picture as a completely fatalistic society in which human will has little or no active role.

The creative social forces within that society also disappear—the forces that actually produced its material needs. Indeed, these forces barely appear in its history at all, even though in reality they were the source of the processes that drove that history forward.
When older and newer traditionalist approaches draw the heritage, and the society that created it, using these features alone, they produce an ideological picture.

That picture indirectly—and sometimes unconsciously—reflects the character of present Arab bourgeois ideology, intertwined with colonial ideology through a long historical relationship between the material foundations of the two.

The picture changes when we look at the heritage through a scientific revolutionary method and through the ideology behind that method—the ideology of the central revolutionary forces in the Arab liberation movement.
Here the heritage comes alive with the movement of the history that produced it.

Its main features are the features of thought in its objective, though indirect, relationship with the movement of that particular society: with its problems, its historical conditions, its contradictions, and the intellectual forms through which different social and ideological struggles were expressed.
Those forms possessed different degrees of relative independence, but they were still connected with the conflicts that produced them.
In this picture, we can see the human forces that act and make history.
We see change and development taking place according to the general laws of social development, interacting in a living way with the internal laws specific to the history of this particular society.
History is not driven by supernatural or fatalistic forces outside human and social action.
At the same time, this picture of the heritage also contains something of the present.
The present appears in it in two connected ways.
First, it appears through the scientific method that allows us to illuminate the heritage within its own historical setting.
Second, it appears through the revolutionary ideology rooted in the social basis of that method.
Traditionalist methods concentrate almost entirely on the supernatural and idealist side of the heritage.
